TileDRAM: Compiler-Controlled Tile-to-DRAM Layouts for 3D DRAM GPGPUs

Guangyuan Xu Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China email: xugy12025@shanghaitech.edu.cn , Lanxuan Zhang Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China email: zhanglx2024@shanghaitech.edu.cn , Ziyang Li Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China email: lizy12024@shanghaitech.edu.cn , Zhaoshi Li Affiliation: MetaX Integrated Circuits (Shanghai) Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China email: zhaoshi.li@metax-tech.com and Yajun Ha Affiliation: ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China email: hayj@shanghaitech.edu.cn
© none
Abstract.

Modern GPU compilers expose rich layout abstractions for mapping tensors to threads and on-chip resources, but compute-unit-local (CU-local) 3D DRAM architectures lack a corresponding abstraction for specifying how operand-tile data are arranged within the DRAM address space. Without such an abstraction, conventional placement under the existing DRAM address mapping can subject structured tile accesses to severe row-buffer conflicts.

We present TileDRAM, a compiler–runtime toolchain that introduces tile-to-DRAM layouts as a compiler-visible abstraction for DRAM placement. TileDRAM extends the GPU Linear Layout abstraction from compute-side mapping targets to DRAM placement coordinates and selects layouts per tile access signature, using recurring tile-local access behavior as the specialization unit. Since row-buffer locality depends on ordered request history, TileDRAM evaluates candidate layouts through their row-buffer behavior under fixed DRAM address mappings. Accesses under the selected layouts are realized through ordinary address arithmetic, without new address-remapping hardware or ISA support.

In full-trace replay on Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 across 108 MoE FFN cases, TileDRAM reduces the request-weighted row-conflict rate from 75.7% to 15.2% and achieves a 1.77×\times geomean speedup. Retargeting six traces to six 3D DRAM organizations yields a 2.20×\times geomean speedup under the same compiler abstraction. On an RTX 3090, address transformation adds 0.17% geomean overhead over identity.

1. Introduction

Memory bandwidth is a first-order system constraint in LLM inference. The pressure is most acute in feed-forward network (FFN) layers, where dense matrix projections dominate data movement at small batch sizes. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, routing activates only a few experts per token, yet each activated expert still performs dense projections over activation and weight tensors (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). On GPUs, these projections execute as grouped or batched tiled general matrix multiplications (GEMMs), whose thread blocks repeatedly fetch operand tiles as they advance along the reduction (K) dimension. These structured tile streams make high-bandwidth 3D DRAM an attractive substrate.

Prior 3D DRAM systems motivate two representative chip-wide abstractions for GPGPUs: using 3D DRAM as the GPU’s global memory (Li et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025) or as a GPU-wide last-level cache (LLC) (Loh and Hill, 2012; Zhao et al., 2019). Using the stack as GPU global memory routes its bandwidth through the package-level endpoint instead of delivering the stack’s high local bandwidth directly, while the LLC abstraction pays network-on-chip (NoC) area and power to distribute that local bandwidth GPU-wide (Kahng et al., 2009). We instead focus on the compute-unit-local (CU-local) organization motivated in Section 2.1, where each CU accesses its nearby 3D DRAM stack through a software-managed address-space aperture served by a local memory controller.

However, this high-bandwidth local path also subjects operand request streams directly to the DRAM controller. Without warp-level request coalescing and traffic attenuation through the on-chip caches, numerous fine-grained and potentially redundant memory requests can propagate to the DRAM subsystem, substantially amplifying contention among concurrent memory requests, and ultimately reducing the effective memory bandwidth available to the application. DRAM service efficiency therefore depends on the row-buffer locality of the resulting row-access sequence.

This dependence on DRAM placement reveals a missing abstraction between compiler-visible tile semantics and DRAM placement: a tile-to-DRAM layout that defines how operand-tile data are arranged within the DRAM address space. Under a fixed DRAM address mapping, the tile-to-DRAM layout determines the physical address stream presented to the memory controller and thereby governs the row-buffer locality of DRAM accesses (Figure 1).

Across our 108 full-trace MoE FFN cases, conventional placement under the fixed DRAM address mapping yields a 75.7% request-weighted row-conflict rate: successive accesses to the same row buffer target different rows, each paying a precharge and an activation.

Modern GPU software stacks offer rich tile-level abstractions for compute-side layout and data movement, but provide no corresponding abstraction for DRAM placement. Triton, CUTLASS, and CuTe provide tiled programming and layout abstractions (Tillet et al., 2019; , 2026; Cecka, 2026), while cuTile, CuTe DSL, TileLang, and Gluon expose tiles directly in their programming abstractions (, 2026; , 2026; Wang et al., 2026; , 2026; Hagedorn et al., 2023). Linear Layouts provide a formal representation of distributed tensor layouts as linear maps between labeled vector spaces over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} (Zhou et al., 2026). Across these systems, the operand tile is already an established compiler-visible unit for specifying layout and data movement. However, these abstractions stop at the compute side: they determine how tile data map to threads, registers, and shared memory, but not how operand-tile data are arranged within the DRAM address space. DRAM placement therefore remains outside the compiler’s tile-level layout abstraction.

Prior work improves row-buffer locality by modifying the DRAM address mapping in the memory controller (Liu et al., 2018; Rotaru et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2022). Application-specific synthesis can optimize one global mapping for a representative workload trace (Rotaru et al., 2025), but that mapping must therefore accommodate the heterogeneous access patterns within the trace (Section 2.3). Independently specializing these patterns at the controller side would require maintaining multiple mapping contexts and selecting the appropriate context for each request (Zhang et al., 2022).

Taken together, these observations yield two key insights. First, CU-local integration provides high local bandwidth, but compiler-awareness of DRAM placement is necessary to fully utilize the bandwidth. Placement should therefore become an explicit compiler-controlled decision. Second, we identify recurring tile-local access behavior as a stable unit for specializing placement. This granularity also aligns naturally with existing GPU software abstractions, where operand tiles are already compiler-visible units for layout and data movement.

Guided by these insights, we propose TileDRAM, a compiler–runtime toolchain that introduces tile-to-DRAM layouts as a compiler-visible abstraction for compiler-controlled DRAM placement. TileDRAM represents this abstraction as tile-to-DRAM Linear Layouts: reusable 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-linear maps that extend the Linear Layout abstraction from compute-side resources to DRAM placement coordinates. Each layout maps logical operand-tile coordinates to DRAM placement coordinates.

Although access behavior varies with operand properties and tile configurations, the same ordered tile-local access behavior recurs across many tile instances. TileDRAM captures this with a tile access signature that combines tile configuration, operand properties, and the ordered tile-local access sequence. The tile-to-DRAM mapping itself is stateless, with each tile coordinate mapped without reference to access history. However, the induced row-buffer behavior is stateful, because whether a request hits an open row depends on preceding requests in the ordered tile-local access sequence. TileDRAM therefore evaluates candidate layouts by simulating row-buffer state transitions under each signature’s ordered access, selecting the layout with the fewest row conflicts.

An offline solver selects reusable layouts for each tile access signature; the compiler applies them during address generation, and the runtime supplies each tile’s placement without new address-remapping hardware or ISA support. Retargeting to different 3D DRAM organizations reselects layouts while reusing the same abstraction and compilation path.

Using NVBit traces of Triton/Gluon kernels (Tillet et al., 2019; , 2026; Villa et al., 2019) replayed with Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 (Khairy et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2024), TileDRAM reduces the request-weighted row-conflict rate from 75.7% to 15.2% and achieves a 1.77×\times geomean kernel speedup across 108 MoE FFN cases. Across six full-trace streams retargeted to six 3D DRAM organizations, TileDRAM reduces row conflicts by 79.2% and achieves a 2.20×\times geomean speedup. On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090, address transformation adds 0.17% geomean overhead over identity across the 108 measured kernel configurations. Together, these results establish compiler-controlled DRAM placement as a new optimization dimension: with the DRAM address mapping left unchanged, the compiler-selected layout alone accounts for the gain.

Our main contributions can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We introduce tile-to-DRAM layouts as a compiler-visible abstraction for DRAM placement, and represent them as tile-to-DRAM Linear Layouts: 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-linear maps that extend GPU Linear Layouts from compute-side resources to DRAM placement coordinates, with tile access signatures as their stable specialization unit.

  • •

    We characterize the row-buffer locality impact of conventional DRAM placement in CU-local 3D DRAM GPGPUs. Across 108 full-trace MoE FFN cases, conventional placement yields a 75.7% request-weighted row-conflict rate, showing that high local bandwidth alone does not ensure efficient DRAM service.

  • •

    We present TileDRAM, a compiler–runtime toolchain that selects a layout per tile access signature, requiring neither address-remapping hardware nor ISA support.

  • •

    We evaluate TileDRAM using a full-trace framework integrating Triton, Accel-Sim, and Ramulator2 across 108 MoE FFN cases plus a six-stream, six-organization retargeting sweep. TileDRAM consistently reduces row conflicts, improves performance, and incurs only 0.17% geomean address-transformation overhead on an RTX 3090.

2. Background and Motivation

2.1. 3D DRAM and the CU-local Architecture

Recent 3D DRAM architectures place multi-tier DRAM structures close to logic through dense vertical integration. In the CU-local organization modeled here, the vertically integrated DRAM structure is connected to a separate logic die through face-to-face Cu–Cu hybrid bonding (Li et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2022; Pan et al., 2025). The logic die can host memory controllers and near-memory compute in recent designs (Li et al., 2025; Nair et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025). This stacked integration provides a high-bandwidth local DRAM–logic path, while a distinct package-level endpoint connects the GPU or xPU to the stack (Li et al., 2025; Nair et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2025).

This separation makes the package-level endpoint the bandwidth boundary for chip-wide access. Stratum reports 19.01–30.34 TB/s of internal bandwidth across its memory tiers (Pan et al., 2025). Exporting a stack through an HBM-style package interface instead offers roughly 0.8–1.2 TB/s per stack in HBM3/HBM3E (, 2025; , 2024), making the package-level endpoint 16–38×\times narrower than the modeled internal path. This gap motivates placing compute near the stack rather than exporting its bandwidth (Li et al., 2025; Pan et al., 2025). Recent industrial inference hardware provides a concrete instance of this CU-local principle. OpenAI’s Jalapeño adopts a memory-sliced architecture in which each compute core slice has a local view of its own HBM4 slice and the chip omits a global last-level cache, avoiding contention on a unified global memory subsystem (Ho et al., 2026). Remote and global memory accesses use a separate general-purpose interconnect.

A transparent GPU-wide LLC offers a contrasting global abstraction: it makes the stack a shared last-level cache reachable from every CU. Requests and responses therefore traverse a chip-wide NoC and arbitration path. The associated routers, buffers, and links consume area and power even when the target cache line resides in that stack (Kahng et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2019). More generally, GPU-global-memory and GPU-wide-LLC organizations place package-level or chip-wide interconnects on the common path to stack-resident data. A CU-local organization instead keeps common accesses within a local compute–memory domain, while retaining a separate path for remote or global communication.

Motivated by this locality-oriented organization, we model the CU-local design shown in Figure 1(b), where each CU accesses its nearby 3D DRAM stack through a local memory controller, and analyze one CU–stack pair at a time. TileDRAM’s architectural boundary is a software-managed CU-local aperture in a dedicated device-physical address space. Requests to this aperture reach the local controller without virtual-address translation, warp-level request coalescing, or caching; all other addresses traverse the conventional memory hierarchy. The local stack remains a conventional banked, row-buffered DRAM system (Mutlu and Moscibroda, 2007; Rixner et al., 2000).

2.2. MoE FFNs Present Structured Operand-Tile Streams

MoE FFNs provide a representative workload for studying DRAM placement within this CU-local boundary: their inference traffic is structured before it becomes a DRAM address stream. Routing activates a small set of expert MLPs for each token, and each activated expert applies dense matrix projections over activation and expert-weight tensors (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). After routing, the active experts can be represented as a group of dense GEMM problems with runtime per-expert row counts:

Cm​n(e)=∑kAm​k(e)​Bk​n(e),0≤m<Me,e∈ℰ.C^{(e)}_{mn}=\sum_{k}A^{(e)}_{mk}B^{(e)}_{kn},\qquad 0\leq m<M_{e},\ e\in\mathcal{E}.

Here, ee identifies an active expert, MeM_{e} its routed-token count, nn the output-feature coordinate, and kk the hidden/reduction coordinate. Each problem retains its own MeM_{e}, the ragged expert dimension left by routing and dispatch (, 2026; , 2026).

Grouped GEMM implementations tile each problem’s (m,n)(m,n) output space into cooperative-thread-array (CTA) work units and advance through kk by repeatedly loading activation and expert-weight tiles (, 2026; , 2026). Each CTA executes on one CU at a time and generates, for each operand stream, an ordered tile-local access sequence of copy events. Dynamic scheduling assigns tile instances to CTAs, and persistent CTAs may process multiple instances. Across the grouped workload, these CTA instances jointly cover each expert problem and may reside on multiple CUs; Figure 2 follows one representative tile instance and its CTA residency on one CU. The resulting kernel presents structured, ordered tile-local access sequences at the CU-local boundary defined above (Figure 2). Runtime scheduling determines how CTAs resident on a CU interleave; this cross-tile interleaving remains separate from each tile’s local access pattern.

Under the standard roofline model (Williams et al., 2009; , 2026), one 2-byte touch of each FP16/BF16 input and output gives the ideal per-expert GEMM intensity:

(1) Iideal=M​K​NM​K+K​N+M​N​FLOP/B,I_{\mathrm{ideal}}=\frac{MKN}{MK+KN+MN}\ \mathrm{FLOP/B},

taking M=MeM=M_{e} for one expert problem. For an FFN projection with K=4096K=4096 and N=14336N=14336, for example, M=64M=64–128128 gives Iideal=62.7I_{\mathrm{ideal}}=62.7–123.1123.1 FLOP/B; our evaluated suite (Section 6.1) spans 55.455.4–123.0123.0 FLOP/B.

Using published dense-compute and external-memory specifications for conventional GPUs (, 2021; , 2022; , 2026), the corresponding GDDR/HBM ridge points are 153–295 FLOP/B. Stratum’s reported 19.01–30.34 TB/s aggregate in-stack bandwidth (Pan et al., 2025) and the H100 whole-GPU peak (, 2026) together give a local-memory ridge reference of 32.6–52.0 FLOP/B. This ratio is unchanged under proportional partitioning of compute throughput and local-memory bandwidth. The evaluated ideal-intensity band therefore lies below conventional GPU ridges but above this local-memory reference.

The local stack nevertheless retains banked, row-buffered DRAM service, so realizing the potential of this high-bandwidth path depends on the row sequence induced by DRAM placement. Across our 108 full-trace MoE FFN cases, conventional placement yields a 75.7% request-weighted row-conflict rate (Section 6.2). Figure 3(a) isolates the mechanism at tile granularity: a repeated tile-local difference maps to repeated row changes, motivating explicit compiler control through a tile-to-DRAM layout.

2.3. Stable Specialization Granularity in MoE FFNs

Application-specific synthesis constructs a workload-tuned controller mapping from representative address differences (Rotaru et al., 2025), shared by all tensor and kernel requests reaching the controller. Two properties of MoE FFN traffic, together with the cost of exhaustive trace-wide controller-map synthesis, make the complete trace an impractical specialization unit.

Heterogeneity appears within a single GEMM. The AA (lhs) operand advances over row and reduction coordinates, the BB (rhs) operand over reduction and output-feature coordinates, and both are loaded in the same reduction loop. One global mapping must therefore serve two distinct address-difference distributions (, 2026; , 2026).

The complete trace also depends on runtime composition: routing sets expert-local workloads, while grouped GEMM uses runtime (M,N,K)(M,N,K) values to form and schedule tiles across problems (Hwang et al., 2023; , 2026; , 2026). Expert-local MM changes the number of tile instances, their source-interval bases, and the interleaving of requests from different tiles (, 2026; , 2026; , 2026).

Trace-wide synthesis is also expensive: because each outer mapping candidate induces a separate trace-dependent fixed-domain problem, exhaustively searching the evaluated mapping families against the Llama 4 full trace requires on the order of 101410^{14} evaluations of candidate copy events before any fixed-domain solve, and every new phase, problem shape, or autotuned tile configuration presents a fresh workload-wide target (Appendix B).

By contrast, the tile-local view is invariant. Once addresses are expressed as source-interval offsets, tile configuration and operand properties fix one ordered tile-local access sequence across instance origins and evaluated MM values (Figure 3). The tile access signature records these fields together with the resulting sequence, so TileDRAM selects one tile-to-DRAM layout per signature (Section 4.1).

3. Overview

TileDRAM realizes compiler-controlled DRAM placement as a target-scoped PLAN–BIND–APPLY lifecycle (Figure 4).  The DRAM configuration fixes the DRAM organization and the controller-owned DRAM address mapping.  A tile access signature combines tile configuration, operand properties, and the ordered tile-local access sequence.  Layout selection evaluates layout candidates over the ordered requests for row reuse and ranks legal candidates by fewer row conflicts, greater parallelism, and lower address-generation complexity.  The selected layout is combined with the DRAM configuration and packaged as a reusable tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout template.  BIND looks up the PLAN-produced template for each tile access signature.  BIND then combines the referenced template with the tile ID, source interval, and the DRAM region to construct a tile descriptor.  During execution, APPLY transforms each source address using a GF(2)-based address transform, then uses the descriptor’s region base to form the backend address.  A new DRAM configuration reruns PLAN; BIND and APPLY remain unchanged.

4. Tile-to-DRAM Linear Layouts

This section develops tile-to-DRAM Linear Layouts as an 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-linear representation of compiler-controlled DRAM placement. For each tile access signature, we formalize how a candidate layout and the signature’s ordered tile-local access sequence jointly determine row-buffer behavior. TileDRAM formulates layout selection as a row-locality optimization subject to the target DRAM address mapping and placement constraints. Each admitted signature yields a reusable tile-to-DRAM layout template for the target contract, used to bind logical tiles to concrete DRAM regions.

4.1. Tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout Object

A tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout maps each layout unit to a row-buffer domain, a row within that domain, and a within-row position. We call the hardware unit that independently holds one open row a row-buffer domain, or simply a domain; in the evaluated 3D organization, a domain is one (tier, bank) pair, but the construction needs only whatever unit the target tracks independently.

TileDRAM reuses the labeled 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} algebra of GPU Linear Layouts for a separate logical-tile-to-DRAM placement map (Zhou et al., 2026). Triton distributed layouts map hardware-resource coordinates to logical tensor coordinates; TileDRAM maps normalized tile coordinates to DRAM placement coordinates. Each recorded access carries a source address sis_{i} in the global space. Let AA denote the source-interval base and gg the granularity of one access. Normalization extracts the layout-unit index ℓi=⌊(si−A)/g⌋\ell_{i}=\lfloor(s_{i}-A)/g\rfloor and within-unit byte offset δi=(si−A)modg\delta_{i}=(s_{i}-A)\bmod g. Writing ri∈𝔽2nr_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} for the 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} encoding of ℓi\ell_{i}, a reusable tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout is the strictly linear map

(2) [pidizi]=Wsem​ri=[WCWDWR]​ri,Wsem∈𝔽2m×n.\begin{bmatrix}p_{i}\\ d_{i}\\ z_{i}\end{bmatrix}=W_{\mathrm{sem}}r_{i}=\begin{bmatrix}W_{C}\\ W_{D}\\ W_{R}\end{bmatrix}r_{i},\qquad W_{\mathrm{sem}}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times n}.

The WDW_{D} slice determines the row-buffer domain, WRW_{R} the row within that domain, and WCW_{C} the within-row position of the layout unit. Equal WDW_{D} images therefore share a domain, while equal (WD,WR)(W_{D},W_{R}) images target the same row. The domain’s current open-row state determines whether a request is a hit, a conflict, or an opening miss. This expresses row locality in the same labeled-map algebra as compute-side layouts.

TileDRAM selects one layout per tile access signature, written θ=(κ,ρ,χ)\theta=(\kappa,\rho,\chi). Here, κ\kappa denotes the tile configuration, comprising tile shape (BM,BN,BK)(B_{M},B_{N},B_{K}), pipeline-stage count (num_stages), and warp count (num_warps); ρ\rho denotes the operand-property tuple, comprising operand position (lhs or rhs), data type (dtype), source-stride pattern (stride), and source layout (row-major or column-major); and χ\chi denotes the ordered tile-local access sequence. A representative execution yields the normalized source sequence SθS_{\theta} for this signature, which is used for layout selection.

Each live layout-unit index ℓi\ell_{i} is injectively encoded as its coordinate rir_{i}; the resulting sequence Sθ=(r0,…,rN−1)S_{\theta}=(r_{0},\ldots,r_{N-1}) is the ordered input to layout selection. We evaluate this construction on tiled GEMM under the conditions stated in Appendix A.8. Figure 5 shows the single-row-buffer projection of the Figure 3 stream under a tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout.

The formal treatment below retains the target’s independent row-buffer domains and their separate open-row states. The map in Eq. (2) defines a static DRAM placement, whereas row-buffer outcomes depend on request order. TileDRAM therefore augments the layout with ordered row-buffer state semantics.

4.2. Ordered Row-Buffer Semantics and Row-Reuse Kernel Reduction

Immediately before request ii, each domain either holds one open row or is closed; write σi​(d)\sigma_{i}(d) for that state, with ⊥\bot denoting closed, and let every domain start closed. Assuming the controller retains open rows across requests, the row-buffer transition over SθS_{\theta} is

(3) ϵi={miss,σi(di)=⊥,hit,σi​(di)=zi,conflict,otherwise,σi+1=σi[di↦zi].\epsilon_{i}=\begin{cases}\mathrm{miss},&\sigma_{i}(d_{i})=\bot,\\ \mathrm{hit},&\sigma_{i}(d_{i})=z_{i},\\ \mathrm{conflict},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\qquad\sigma_{i+1}=\sigma_{i}[d_{i}\mapsto z_{i}].

An opening miss is the “row closed” case of classic memory schedulers (Mutlu and Moscibroda, 2007) and pays one activation; a conflict requires a precharge and an activation before that request can be served; a hit requires neither. TileDRAM’s source-order objective minimizes conflicts first; the remaining selection criteria are defined in Section 4.3.

For a fixed domain projection WDW_{D}, the row-reuse kernel

K=ker⁡[WDWR]K=\ker\!\begin{bmatrix}W_{D}\\ W_{R}\end{bmatrix}

Intervening requests to other domains do not change this state. Thus, the source-order hit/miss/conflict classification is fixed by the source order and layout before scheduler effects. The target organization bounds how many bits may name a domain (bb) and how many may name a row within it (rrowr_{\mathrm{row}}). This reduction requires three properties, each formalized and proved in the appendix. Sequence recurrence: a signature determines one ordered coordinate sequence, so one representative profile applies across its admitted instances (Appendix A.8). Mapping consistency: within the admitted bit-selection-and-XOR family, DRAM placement and the target DRAM address mapping compose into an affine 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} map whose domain- and row-equality relations agree with those resolved by the controller (Appendix A.1). Binding legality: reused bindings retain the signature’s source interpretation and request formation, realize those labels consistently, and satisfy the placement bounds, so every admitted tile placement reproduces the selected row behavior (Appendix A.3).

For a fixed WDW_{D}, row sublayouts whose joint domain–row maps have the same kernel induce the same domain-local row-equality relation, so the inner search can operate on subspaces KK rather than on matrix representations of WRW_{R}. Once the three properties hold, maximizing row hits over placements therefore reduces exactly to choosing the maximum-weight cc-dimensional subspace, giving the fixed-domain objective

(4) max⁡∑Δ∈KK⊆ker⁡(WD),dimK=c⁡wWD​(Δ).\max_{K\subseteq\ker(W_{D}),\ \dim K=c}\sum_{\Delta\in K}w_{W_{D}}(\Delta).

Rotaru et al. formulate the same subspace-selection problem (Rotaru et al., 2025).

The two formulations reverse which map is the decision variable: Rotaru et al. synthesize the controller address map with data placement fixed, whereas TileDRAM synthesizes data placement with the controller mapping fixed. This is a reversal of the control variable, rather than an algebraic duality. GPU Linear Layouts make that decision variable expressible: the layout algebra that compilers already use for lanes and registers now extends to row-buffer domains and rows, turning DRAM placement into a compiler-visible decision variable. Taking differences over tile-local access coordinates rather than a flat trace then lets one solution serve every tile sharing the signature.

The objective optimizes the layout under each signature’s ordered tile-local access sequence. The predecessor, hit, and coordinate-lifting derivations appear in Appendices A.4–A.5.

4.3. Layout Synthesis and Selection

Because WDW_{D} determines predecessors within each row-buffer domain and thus wWDw_{W_{D}}, Eq. (4) is evaluated for each fixed domain projection. The resulting five-stage construction forms the layout-selection core of PLAN and produces an executable layout from SθS_{\theta} and the target organization.

  1. (1)

    Row-buffer-domain projection. Enumerate a finite target-specific family of row-buffer-domain sublayouts WDW_{D}. Each candidate assigns source coordinates to the row buffers independently tracked by the organization; the catalog holds bit-selection and constrained structured-XOR candidates.

  2. (2)

    Kernel construction. Form predecessor differences within each row-buffer domain and solve Eq. (4) for a cc-dimensional row-reuse kernel KK.

  3. (3)

    Layout completion. Reconstruct a row sublayout WRW_{R} whose joint row-buffer-domain and row map has kernel exactly KK using the sparse construction of Rotaru et al. (Rotaru et al., 2025), then add WCW_{C} to bring WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}} to full column rank.

  4. (4)

    Physical realization. Express WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}} in the target’s address basis to obtain the executable WphysW_{\mathrm{phys}}, then derive its byte-placement rule. In this basis, the fixed address mapping recovers the intended row-buffer-domain and row labels, and ordinary bit operations generate the backend offset. Retained candidates are injective on live coordinates and satisfy mapping consistency (Appendix A.1) together with alignment, capacity, CU-local aperture bounds, and allocation-policy constraints (Appendix A.3).

  5. (5)

    Ordered selection. Run the row-state transition of Eq. (3) on every retained layout. Selection first minimizes source-order conflicts. Among equal-conflict layouts, it favors greater source-sequence domain coverage, measured by 𝖼𝗈𝗏⁡(S,WD)\mathsf{cov}(S,W_{D}) in Appendix A.2, and then lower nonzero-term complexity of the executable address map.

The outer loop exhaustively enumerates the finite domain-projection family. For each WDW_{D}, the exact route finds the optimum of Eq. (4), while the greedy route returns a feasible kernel (Appendix A.5). Reconstruction and legality filtering retain only candidates satisfying live-coordinate injectivity, target mapping consistency, and binding legality. The retained candidates are ranked exhaustively by the lexicographic objective (Appendices A.6–A.7) within the enumerated candidate family. The selected WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}} is realized in the target address basis and reused across legal tile placements.

5. Compiler and Runtime Realization

The target-specific tile-to-DRAM layout template developed in Section 4 is realized through the three-stage PLAN–BIND–APPLY lifecycle. PLAN selects and realizes the template. BIND spans compilation and runtime: compiler-side BIND performs template lookup, emits binding metadata, and marks the corresponding accesses for APPLY; runtime BIND uses that metadata to construct a tile descriptor for a resident tile (a concrete tile instance placed in a DRAM region). During execution, APPLY consumes that descriptor to transform each active lane’s source address; GPU execution and replay use the same address transformation. In the evaluated Ampere-class realization, operand-tile loads use cp.async lowered to LDGSTS.128. Figure 6 isolates this compiler/replay address equivalence, and Appendix C shows the programmer-facing kernel entry.

5.1. Semantic Extraction and Offline Template Construction

Programming interface.

TileDRAM does not require programmers to name DRAM banks, rows, or address-map bits. The programmer-facing annotation supplies problem, tile, execution, and operand properties, while the kernel body remains ordinary Triton/Gluon code (Appendix C); DRAM placement remains TileDRAM-managed rather than part of the kernel’s logical tile specification.

Semantic extraction.

From the tiled-kernel representation, the compiler derives the tile configuration and operand properties. A recorded representative active-lane sequence supplies the ordered tile-local access sequence; together, these fields form the tile access signature. Normalization relative to the source interval (Section 4) yields the representative normalized source sequence used by PLAN. For each admitted signature and target contract, PLAN synthesizes the layout and its target-specific layout realization, publishing one reusable template keyed by the signature.

5.2. Template Binding and Address Lowering

Tile binding (BIND)

On the compiler side, BIND performs template lookup for each admitted tile access signature and records a reference to the corresponding target-specific layout template produced by PLAN, together with the rule for deriving the tile ID from the execution context. A tile ID identifies an operand tile within the current GEMM instance. For GEMM, the lhs and rhs tile IDs are represented by the operand-tile coordinates (im,ik)(i_{m},i_{k}) and (ik,in)(i_{k},i_{n}), respectively. When the tile is placed in a DRAM region, the compiler-defined tile-ID rule yields the concrete tile ID from the current execution context, and runtime BIND obtains the referenced template from this binding metadata and combines it with the tile ID, source interval [A,A+E)[A,A+E), and concrete DRAM region to construct a tile descriptor for the resident tile. Each admitted resident tile uses one tile access signature and one corresponding target-specific layout template throughout its residency, so its descriptor remains fixed and is reused by accesses to the same resident tile. Thus, lhs accesses from CTAs that differ only in ini_{n}, and rhs accesses from CTAs that differ only in imi_{m}, resolve to the same tile descriptor. At execution, runtime BIND provides the descriptor for the current resident tile as input to APPLY.

Address lowering (APPLY)

At compilation, the compiler places APPLY after the source pointer tensor is formed by address arithmetic for each admitted tile access. At execution, the path uses the tile descriptor for the current resident tile to transform each active lane’s source address for its 16-byte LDGSTS.128 transfer. The transformation follows three ordered stages: Extract each source address relative to the source interval, yielding the layout-unit index and within-unit byte offset; Transform the layout unit through the descriptor’s target-specific layout realization; and Reconstruct the backend address from the transformed unit, unchanged byte offset, and region base before the copy. Per-lane integer and pointer operations realize this software-selected placement through ordinary address generation, requiring no new address-remapping hardware or ISA support. The formal address contract is given in Appendix A.1, and the binding metadata and address-lowering sequence appear in Appendix C. Only operand accesses with a tile descriptor are redirected to their assigned DRAM regions, while ordinary loads and stores retain the conventional memory path.

5.3. Runtime Replay and Simulator Execution

Simulator replay represents each dynamic tile access as an ordered tile-local access sequence of active-lane asynchronous-copy events (LDGSTS.128) carrying source address sis_{i} and event metadata ηi\eta_{i}. Here, ηi\eta_{i} denotes the event’s identity, destination, dependency, and request attributes. Runtime scheduling may interleave ordered tile-local access sequences from resident tiles while preserving the event order within each sequence. Each sequence carries the descriptor for its resident tile as input to the APPLY path.

For each asynchronous-copy event, the simulator evaluates the same address transformation specified by APPLY using the descriptor for the sequence’s resident tile. It carries the resulting backend address together with the event metadata into replay. Replay uses the descriptor’s template and placement while preserving event metadata and dependency. The production compiler lowering and simulator-side transformer implement one common address function, checked against an independent reference evaluator. Appendix D reports the covered configurations, address-function families, and byte addresses. Each transformed asynchronous-copy event forms one CU-local DRAM request in the Ramulator2 replay. Ramulator2’s fixed address mapper and controller advance row-buffer state and return service latency to GPGPU-Sim, which applies it to the originating asynchronous-copy dependency.

6. Evaluation

6.1. Experimental Setup

Simulation and replay protocol.

We evaluate TileDRAM with traces collected from Triton/Gluon tiled GEMM kernels using NVBit (Tillet et al., 2019; , 2026; Villa et al., 2019) and replayed through Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 (Khairy et al., 2020; Luo et al., 2024) on one CU and its paired 3D DRAM stack. Each baseline–TileDRAM pair holds the logical event trace, target organization, the initial closed-row state, and refresh/precharge policy fixed while varying DRAM placement. Layout selection uses the ordered tile-local access sequence, whereas replay counters follow FR-FCFS service order. Before replay, we verify that the compiler lowering and simulator transformer produce the same addresses as the canonical byte-address function in Appendix A.1.

The evaluation covers 108 full-trace MoE FFN cases spanning Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025), DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026), Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), Hunyuan-A13B (Tencent Hunyuan Team, 2025), and Llama 4 (Meta AI, 2025), across up/gate and down projections and eight tile shapes. The same 108 kernel configurations provide hardware-cost calibration; a separate sweep covers 36 full-trace stream–organization pairs. All reported TileDRAM layouts use the same greedy selection route (Appendix A.5). We report row-conflict rates from pooled row events and speedup as the geometric mean of per-case baseline-to-TileDRAM cycle ratios. Per-case synthesis time and peak resident memory measure offline layout-selection cost; address-transformation cost is measured separately on RTX 3090 hardware. The primary 3D DRAM configuration uses 8 tiers, 16 banks, 13 row bits, and 3 column bits with RoBaTiCoCh address mapping, OpenRowPolicy, and FR-FCFS scheduling.

6.2. RQ1: Row-Buffer Cost of Conventional DRAM Placement

Figure 7 reports a 75.7% request-weighted row-conflict rate across all 108 cases. Per-case rates span 15.9–98.8% and family-pooled rates 56.9–95.1%, while the M=64M=64 and M=128M=128 groups differ little (73.9% and 76.7%). The remaining variation follows model family, projection type, and tile configuration, whose ordered tile-local access sequences induce different domain and row trajectories under the target DRAM address mapping. The baseline pathology reflects two interacting properties of GEMM execution. First, its operand-local address structure is misaligned with the controller’s fixed address-field interpretation: regular tile-coordinate changes repeatedly revisit one row-buffer domain at different rows. Second, cp.async exposes these loads through a lane- and warp-interleaved issue order rather than a complete tensor-row scan, separating accesses that could reuse an open row. The mapping fixes the domain/row relation, while this issue order determines when it is exposed, producing repeated precharge–activate transitions and row conflicts. FR-FCFS can reorder ready requests, but cannot change the assigned domain or row.

Average read latency correspondingly ranges from 41.1 to 101.9 GPU cycles and closely tracks row-conflict rate (Pearson r=0.97r=0.97). Because placement shapes the row sequence each domain sees, the suite-wide prevalence of conflicts motivates treating DRAM placement as a software optimization target, while the case-level variation motivates layout selection per tile access signature.

6.3. RQ2: Row-Buffer Locality and Performance

TileDRAM converts a large fraction of suite-wide row conflicts into row hits. Across the 108 cases in Figure 8(a), the request-weighted row-conflict rate falls from 75.7% to 15.2%, an 80.0% pooled reduction, while the row-hit rate rises from 19.3% to 81.6%. Conflict rates fall for every model family, MM value, and tile shape. Family-pooled TileDRAM conflict rates remain within 10.8%–21.2%, compared with 56.9%–95.1% under conventional placement. Layout selection per tile access signature therefore adapts to the access-pattern heterogeneity measured in RQ1 and produces consistently high row locality.

TileDRAM reshapes each operand stream’s row-buffer-domain and row sequence. Many same-domain requests therefore hit open rows, replacing a substantial fraction of precharge–activate transitions with row-hit service. Across cases, the median reductions in ACT and PRE command counts are 78.7% and 82.2%, respectively (IQRs: 65.7–84.6% and 70.5–87.8%). Request-weighted read latency falls from 81.0 to 40.8 GPU cycles, and foreground queue wait falls from 37.3 to 24.9 cycles.

Earlier DRAM completions release asynchronous-copy dependencies sooner, reducing pooled shader memory-stall cycles from 2.086 to 0.962 billion. Speedup then spans 1.10×\times–2.95×\times, with a 1.77×\times geomean across all 108 cases. Across cases, the percentage-point reduction in row-conflict rate tracks the cycle reduction in read latency (r=0.96r=0.96); relative latency and stall reductions track each other (r=0.89r=0.89), and relative stall reduction tracks speedup (r=0.90r=0.90).

The performance range reflects the fraction of each baseline execution occupied by memory stalls. For the 64×128×6464{\times}128{\times}64 tile, the row-conflict rate falls from 87.5% to 11.9%; memory stalls occupy 92.0% of baseline cycles, and cases using this tile achieve a 2.17×\times geomean speedup. For 128×256×64128{\times}256{\times}64, conflicts fall from 74.7% to 12.4%; with a 58.6% baseline stall share, cases using this tile achieve a 1.25×\times geomean speedup. Thus, TileDRAM consistently shortens DRAM service, while the baseline memory-stall share sets the headroom for speedup.

6.4. RQ3: Retargeting Across 3D DRAM Organizations

TileDRAM preserves row locality when retargeted across the evaluated 3D DRAM organizations. We evaluate six full-trace FFN streams with the 64×64×3264{\times}64{\times}32 tile across six target organizations, for 36 paired replays. TileDRAM reselects a legal tile-to-DRAM layout for each target organization.

Across the sweep, the pooled row-conflict rate falls from 84.3% to 17.6%, a 79.2% reduction (Figure 9). These reductions yield a 2.20×\times geomean speedup across the 36 paired replays.

Across organizations, six-stream geomean speedups range from 1.52×\times to 2.77×\times, while pooled-cycle speedups range from 1.60×\times to 3.32×\times. The resulting locality is stable across the evaluated organizations, while baseline conflict headroom and organization-specific DRAM service together determine how that locality translates into cycles. Organization-specific layout selection therefore preserves row locality even as the DRAM address mapping repartitions the physical address space.

6.5. RQ4: Cost of Layout Synthesis and Address Transformation

RQ4 measures both the one-time cost of synthesizing a layout and the dynamic cost of realizing it through compiler-lowered address transformations. Offline synthesis runs once per case and produces the layouts for its tile access signatures; the selected templates are reused across matching dynamic tile instances. We record per-case solver wall time and peak resident memory across 108 cases. Each case compares identity address generation (H​1H1) with the selected transformation (H​2H2). The selected layouts lower to sparse XOR, grouped bit-permutation, and identity paths using shifts, masks, XORs, and address arithmetic. We report the overhead as median⁡(H​2)/median⁡(H​1)−1\operatorname{median}(H2)/\operatorname{median}(H1)-1 and aggregate the corresponding ratios geometrically (Appendix D).

Offline synthesis has a median per-case runtime of 349.0 s and a median peak resident memory of 227.0 MB. Across all 108 hardware-measured kernel configurations, the selected transformations add 0.17% geomean overhead relative to identity address generation; the median is below 0.01%, the 95th percentile is 0.57%, and the maximum is 4.93%. Overall, 104 of 108 cases lie within ±\pm1% and 106 lie within ±\pm2%; the Qwen3.5 down-projection configurations account for the high-overhead tail.

7. Related Work

3D DRAM Architectures and Accelerators.

Vertical integration and hybrid bonding place high-bandwidth memory close to compute, motivating architectures that exploit local memory–logic bandwidth for LLM and MoE inference. H2-LLM co-designs heterogeneous hardware and dataflow around hybrid-bonded memory (Li et al., 2025), HybridSpec combines such memory with heterogeneous execution and speculative decoding (Huang et al., 2026), Stratum uses tiered monolithic 3D DRAM and expert placement for MoE serving (Pan et al., 2025), and Raptor demonstrates an early-silicon 3D-DRAM accelerator (Nair et al., 2026). At industrial scale, OpenAI’s Jalapeño pairs compute core slices with local HBM4 slices in a memory-sliced organization (Ho et al., 2026). Other designs explore hybrid NVM–DRAM, processing-in-memory, and near-memory parallelism (He et al., 2026; Huang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026). These systems establish the architectural substrate for TileDRAM; TileDRAM instead exposes how operand tiles are placed within local DRAM as a compiler-visible layout decision.

Compute-Side Tile Layouts and Algebraic Layout Abstractions.

Modern GPU programming systems make tiled tensor organization and layout first-class abstractions: CUTLASS and Triton support tiled computation, while CuTe provides composable tensor layouts and layout algebra (Cecka, 2026; , 2026; Tillet et al., 2019). Graphene represents multidimensional data and threads as hierarchically tiled first-class tensors, expressing optimized GPU computations as mappings between data and thread tiles (Hagedorn et al., 2023). Gluon exposes explicit tensor layouts for low-level control, and Jalapeño uses Gluon to program its spatial architecture (Ho et al., 2026; , 2026). Linear Layouts provide an algebraic representation for such compute-side layouts, mapping hardware-resource coordinates to logical tensor coordinates over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} (Zhou et al., 2026). TileDRAM extends this abstraction to DRAM placement coordinates, making tile-to-DRAM placement a compiler-visible layout decision.

Controller Mapping and Software-Directed DRAM Placement.

Permutation-based interleaving distributes pages across DRAM structures (Zhang et al., 2000); Liu et al. (Liu et al., 2018) propose PAE, an XOR-based mapping that improves bank/channel parallelism while preserving row-buffer locality; SDAM exposes software-configurable mappings for a 3D memory controller (Zhang et al., 2022); Rotaru et al. synthesize an application-specific mapping over 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2} from a representative application trace (Rotaru et al., 2025); and FACIL selects a mapping for each huge page (Seo et al., 2025). These approaches treat the controller mapping as the decision variable. A single workload-specific mapping must serve heterogeneous accesses, while specializing different access patterns requires multiple mapping contexts and controller-side selection support. Software-directed placement instead chooses where data reside, at page (Agarwal et al., 2015), DNN-layer (Pandey and Panda, 2024), region (Khadirsharbiyani et al., 2022), or stream (Li et al., 2024) granularity; the stream-based design also controls element order and cache placement in a distributed DRAM cache. TileDRAM keeps the controller mapping fixed and instead specializes data placement using recurring ordered tile-local access behavior. Many tile access signatures can therefore coexist under one mapping, with each placement realized through ordinary address arithmetic and without controller or ISA changes.

8. Conclusion and Future Work

TileDRAM shows that DRAM placement can be an explicit compiler-controlled tile layout decision while the memory-controller address mapping remains fixed. Building on recurring tile-local access behavior as a stable specialization unit, it extends GPU Linear Layouts to represent reusable tile-to-DRAM placements selected per tile access signature. The resulting compiler–runtime toolchain realizes these layouts through ordinary address arithmetic, without new ISA support or remapping hardware. Across 108 full-trace MoE FFN cases, TileDRAM reduces the request-weighted row-conflict rate from 75.7% to 15.2% and achieves a 1.77×\times geomean speedup; retargeting across six 3D DRAM organizations yields a 2.20×\times geomean speedup, while address transformation adds 0.17% overhead on an RTX 3090.

Our evaluation focuses on tiled GEMM within one CU–stack pair, with the 3D DRAM memory system evaluated through trace-driven Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 replay. Future work includes extending TileDRAM to other kernels, such as attention and convolution, coordinating layouts across multiple CU–stack pairs, and validating compiler-controlled placement on physical 3D DRAM systems.

Appendix A Tile-to-DRAM Layout Details

This appendix formalizes the source interface for tile access, the semantic tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout in a fixed target contract, the layout’s resident tiles and their DRAM regions, the intrinsic ordered row-buffer trajectory and its physical realization, and the reconstruction of a realizable layout from its projected row-reuse kernel. The projected reduction, fixed-domain solver interface, kernel-to-layout reconstruction, and finite-catalog correctness are developed in Appendices A.4–A.7.

Throughout this appendix, we fix one target contract and one tile access signature θ\theta. Thus the access quantum, request-formation policy, target mapping, selection parameters, and placement constraints are standing assumptions rather than arguments repeated in every expression. We write 𝖽𝗋𝖺𝗆⁡(⋅)\mathsf{dram}(\cdot) for the fixed target DRAM address mapping.

A.1. Tile-to-DRAM Semantics

Normalized access sequence.

A signature θ=(κ,ρ,χ)\theta=(\kappa,\rho,\chi) identifies the tile configuration κ\kappa, the operand-property tuple ρ\rho, and the ordered tile-local access sequence χ\chi. For one representative access sequence of source addresses (s0,…,sN−1)(s_{0},\ldots,s_{N-1}) over interval [A,A+E)[A,A+E), where gg divides EE, access granularity gg gives

ℓi\displaystyle\ell_{i} =⌊si−Ag⌋,\displaystyle=\left\lfloor\frac{s_{i}-A}{g}\right\rfloor, δi\displaystyle\delta_{i} =(si−A)modg,\displaystyle=(s_{i}-A)\bmod g,
ri\displaystyle r_{i} =Λθ​(ℓi),\displaystyle=\Lambda_{\theta}(\ell_{i}), S\displaystyle S =(r0,…,rN−1).\displaystyle=(r_{0},\ldots,r_{N-1}).

The fixed signature θ\theta, under the standing request-formation policy, determines both the source interpretation and event order. Hence Λθ\Lambda_{\theta} maps each observed unit index directly to its normalized coordinate, and SS is the only sequence consumed by layout selection.

We require Λθ\Lambda_{\theta} to be injective on the observed indices {ℓi∣0≤i<N}\{\ell_{i}\mid 0\leq i<N\}.

A different tile placement jj uses its own source base A(j)A^{(j)}, but every admitted instance of the fixed signature yields the same sequence SS. Thus absolute addresses and runtime interleaving may change without changing the input to offline layout selection associated with that tile access signature.

For x∈𝔽2nx\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, a reusable tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout is the block-structured map

Wsem​x=[WC​xWD​xWR​x],Wsem∈𝔽2m×n.W_{\mathrm{sem}}x=\begin{bmatrix}W_{C}x\\ W_{D}x\\ W_{R}x\end{bmatrix},\qquad W_{\mathrm{sem}}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times n}.

The three blocks select the residual address coordinate, row-buffer domain, and row within that domain. If the candidate uses bb independent domain bits and rrowr_{\mathrm{row}} additional row bits, then WC∈𝔽2(m−b−rrow)×nW_{C}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{(m-b-r_{\mathrm{row}})\times n}, WD∈𝔽2b×nW_{D}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{b\times n}, and WR∈𝔽2rrow×nW_{R}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{\mathrm{row}}\times n}, with rank⁡(WD)=b\operatorname{rank}(W_{D})=b and rank⁡([WD;WR])=b+rrow\operatorname{rank}([W_{D};W_{R}])=b+r_{\mathrm{row}}. Every retained executable layout has full column rank; Appendix A.6 constructs such a completion.

Lemma 2 constructs one invertible target-basis matrix G∈𝔽2m×mG\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m} whose domain and row blocks preserve the fixed mapper’s domain and row equality relations.

We use WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}} directly for the reusable semantic layout. For this layout, β=(A,E,B)\beta=(A,E,B) denotes one tile-placement record: source interval [A,A+E)[A,A+E) and region base BB. The fixed context and signature need not be encoded explicitly in either object.

Proposition 1 (compiler composition closure).

Let PP denote the compiler’s composed Linear Layout from compute coordinates to the normalized coordinates rir_{i}. Then Wsem​PW_{\mathrm{sem}}P, its three output blocks, and Wphys​PW_{\mathrm{phys}}P are Linear Layouts. Distinct coordinates in im⁡(P)\operatorname{im}(P) remain distinct exactly when

ker⁡(Wsem)∩im⁡(P)={0}.\ker(W_{\mathrm{sem}})\cap\operatorname{im}(P)=\{0\}.

Canonical byte-address placement.

The target supplies a fixed output translation tρt_{\rho} and a byte-placement function Πρ\Pi_{\rho} whose outputs are gg-aligned byte offsets. For each source address s∈[A,A+E)s\in[A,A+E), the bound layout computes

ℓ=⌊s−Ag⌋,δ=(s−A)modg,r=Λθ(ℓ),y=Wphysr⊕tρ,𝖺𝖽𝖽𝗋(s;Wsem,β)=B+Πρ(y)+δ.\begin{gathered}\ell=\left\lfloor\dfrac{s-A}{g}\right\rfloor,\qquad\delta=(s-A)\bmod g,\qquad r=\Lambda_{\theta}(\ell),\\ y=W_{\mathrm{phys}}r\oplus t_{\rho},\qquad\mathsf{addr}(s;W_{\mathrm{sem}},\beta)=B+\Pi_{\rho}(y)+\delta.\end{gathered}

The within-unit byte offset δ\delta is retained after layout placement. A legal tile placement keeps it within the byte/column position of the same target domain and row; Πρ\Pi_{\rho} must also be in bounds and injective on the translated live image. Request formation converts the resulting byte address into a request for the fixed DRAM address mapping 𝖽𝗋𝖺𝗆\mathsf{dram}.

Lemma 1 (output-translation invariance).

For a fixed output translation tt,

(Wphys​x⊕t)⊕(Wphys​x′⊕t)\displaystyle(W_{\mathrm{phys}}x\oplus t)\oplus(W_{\mathrm{phys}}x^{\prime}\oplus t) =Wphys​(x⊕x′),\displaystyle=W_{\mathrm{phys}}(x\oplus x^{\prime}),
Wphys​x⊕t=Wphys​x′⊕t\displaystyle W_{\mathrm{phys}}x\oplus t=W_{\mathrm{phys}}x^{\prime}\oplus t ⟺Wphys​x=Wphys​x′.\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow W_{\mathrm{phys}}x=W_{\mathrm{phys}}x^{\prime}.

Thus output translation preserves injectivity, pairwise differences, and equality. Under the affine mapping-consistency conditions below, it only relabels mapped domains and rows, so row-state classification remains a property of WDW_{D} and WRW_{R}.

Definition 2 (ordered row-buffer semantics).

A bound instance is request-formation preserving when it forms one physical request qiq_{i} for each normalized event, in the same source order and with rir_{i} as its coordinate ancestry. Physical addresses may vary across tile placements; the common ordered sequence remains SS. Define the semantic domain and row labels

𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍⁡(S,Wsem)=(Nconf​(S,Wsem),Nmiss​(S,Wsem)).\mathsf{rowcnt}(S,W_{\mathrm{sem}})=\bigl(N_{\mathrm{conf}}(S,W_{\mathrm{sem}}),N_{\mathrm{miss}}(S,W_{\mathrm{sem}})\bigr).

Thus, 𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍\mathsf{rowcnt} characterizes the intrinsic source-order row-buffer behavior of the semantic layout.

For physical request qiq_{i}, write 𝖽𝗋𝖺𝗆⁡(qi)=(diphys,ziphys,…)\mathsf{dram}(q_{i})=(d_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}},z_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}},\ldots), where diphysd_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}} and ziphysz_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}} are its resolved physical domain and row. diphys=djphys\displaystyle d_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}}=d_{j}^{\mathrm{phys}} ⟺di=dj,\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow d_{i}=d_{j},
(7) di=dj\displaystyle d_{i}=d_{j} ⟹(ziphys=zjphys⟺zi=zj).\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\bigl(z_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}}=z_{j}^{\mathrm{phys}}\Longleftrightarrow z_{i}=z_{j}\bigr).

Proposition 2 (semantic–mapped-label source-order equivalence).

Let β\beta be a mapping-consistent, request-formation-preserving tile placement of WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}}. Apply the transition in Eq. (6) to its mapped labels (diphys,ziphys)(d_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}},z_{i}^{\mathrm{phys}}) and call the resulting conflict and miss counts

(8) 𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍phys​(S,Wsem,β)=𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍⁡(S,Wsem).\mathsf{rowcnt}^{\mathrm{phys}}(S,W_{\mathrm{sem}},\beta)=\mathsf{rowcnt}(S,W_{\mathrm{sem}}).

The semantic and physical domain labels agree up to the bijective relabeling in Definition 3.

Proof. Both executions start with all domains closed. By Eq. (7), they select corresponding domains and test the same within-domain row equality at request ii. They therefore emit the same event and open corresponding rows. Induction proves identical event sequences and preserves the realized domain labels up to relabeling. □\square

Lemma 2 (affine target factorization).

Suppose the within-unit byte offset affects only the byte/column position, while byte placement, request formation, and the fixed DRAM address mapping make the physical row-buffer-domain and row labels affine in y=Wphys​x⊕tρy=W_{\mathrm{phys}}x\oplus t_{\rho} on the admitted image. G=[GCGDGR]∈𝔽2m×m,row⁡(GD)=row⁡(FD),row⁡(GDGR)=row⁡(FDFR).\begin{gathered}G=\begin{bmatrix}G_{C}\\ G_{D}\\ G_{R}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{m\times m},\\ \operatorname{row}(G_{D})=\operatorname{row}(F_{D}),\\ \operatorname{row}\!\begin{pmatrix}G_{D}\\ G_{R}\end{pmatrix}=\operatorname{row}\!\begin{pmatrix}F_{D}\\ F_{R}\end{pmatrix}.\end{gathered}

The two row-space equalities make GDG_{D} preserve exactly the physical domain-equality relation and make [GD;GR][G_{D};G_{R}] preserve exactly the joint domain–row equality relation. Thus same-WDW_{D} predecessors are exactly predecessors in the same physical row-buffer domain, and WRW_{R} equality within a domain is exactly physical row equality. The weighted kernel therefore counts the intrinsic source-order row hits of every certified realization, while Proposition 2 preserves the source-order domain labels and row-buffer events.

A.2. Source-Sequence Domain Coverage

Source-sequence domain coverage ranks layouts after source-order row conflicts have been minimized. It counts the independent row-buffer domains exercised by the complete source sequence.

Definition 4 (source-sequence domain coverage).

For semantic labels di=WD​rid_{i}=W_{D}r_{i} and ordered sequence S=(r0,…,rN−1)S=(r_{0},\ldots,r_{N-1}), assume N>0N>0.

Define the realized domain set and its coverage score as

(9) 𝒟⁡(S,WD)\displaystyle\mathcal{D}(S,W_{D}) ={WD​ri∣0≤i<N},\displaystyle=\{W_{D}r_{i}\mid 0\leq i<N\},
𝖼𝗈𝗏⁡(S,WD)\displaystyle\mathsf{cov}(S,W_{D}) =|𝒟⁡(S,WD)|.\displaystyle=|\mathcal{D}(S,W_{D})|.

The score counts the distinct domains retained by the complete source-order sequence. Under the closed-domain initial state of Definition 2, this same distinct-domain count is also the opening-miss count established in Appendix A.4. The selector therefore uses row conflicts as its locality criterion and this coverage score as the next criterion. Let

(10) 𝒞conf​(S)=arg​minW∈𝒲cert⁡Nconf​(S,W),\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{conf}}(S)=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}}}N_{\mathrm{conf}}(S,W),

where the minimization ranges over the retained candidate family. Selection then chooses

(11) W⋆∈arg​maxW∈𝒞conf​(S)⁡𝖼𝗈𝗏​(S,WD),W^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{W\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{conf}}(S)}\mathsf{cov}(S,W_{D}),

before minimizing the executable map’s nonzero-term complexity. Thus, among layouts with identical conflict counts, the selected layout exercises the largest number of distinct domains in the source sequence. The score depends only on (S,WD)(S,W_{D}), and Proposition 2 preserves it in every certified physical realization.

A.3. Legal Placement and Allocation Invariance

A reusable layout must assign distinct live bytes to distinct backend addresses and remain valid across the region bases admitted by the allocation policy.

Proposition 3 (address uniqueness).

Let WsemW_{\mathrm{sem}} have full column rank. Suppose Λθ\Lambda_{\theta} is injective on the observed unit indices, the region base BB and byte placement Πρ\Pi_{\rho} are gg-aligned, and Πρ\Pi_{\rho} is injective on the translated live image. If the placement remains in bounds, then the byte-address function

𝖺𝖽𝖽𝗋⁡(⋅,Wsem,β)\mathsf{addr}(\cdot;W_{\mathrm{sem}},\beta) is injective over live layout units and their within-unit byte offsets.

Proof. If two backend addresses are equal, alignment and reduction modulo gg give δ=δ′\delta=\delta^{\prime}. Cancelling the common base and offset, then using injectivity of Πρ\Pi_{\rho}, gives Wphys​r⊕tρ=Wphys​r′⊕tρW_{\mathrm{phys}}r\oplus t_{\rho}=W_{\mathrm{phys}}r^{\prime}\oplus t_{\rho}. The translation cancels, and

Wphys=G−1​WsemW_{\mathrm{phys}}=G^{-1}W_{\mathrm{sem}} has full column rank, so r=r′r=r^{\prime}. Injectivity of Λθ\Lambda_{\theta} then gives the same source-relative unit; together with δ=δ′\delta=\delta^{\prime}, this gives the same source byte. □\square

Definition 5 (legal allocation placement class).

For a semantic layout WW, let Γ⁡(W)\Gamma(W) be the set of tile placements β=(A,E,B)\beta=(A,E,B) whose source interpretation and access quantum match the fixed signature, whose byte placement satisfies Proposition 3 and remains inside the reserved CU-local aperture, and whose physical mapping satisfies Definition 3. DRAM regions of simultaneously resident tiles must be disjoint.

A candidate family is request-formation stable when every β∈Γ⁡(W)\beta\in\Gamma(W) is request-formation preserving in the sense of Definition 2, for every WW in the family.

Let 𝒲cert\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}} denote the finite certified catalog retained by the declared synthesis policy. Every W∈𝒲certW\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}} has a nonempty set Γ⁡(W)\Gamma(W) and stable request formation.

Corollary 1 (allocation invariance).

For any W∈𝒲certW\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}} and any two tile placements β1,β2∈Γ⁡(W)\beta_{1},\beta_{2}\in\Gamma(W),

𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍phys​(S,W,β1)\displaystyle\mathsf{rowcnt}^{\mathrm{phys}}(S,W,\beta_{1}) =𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍⁡(S,W)\displaystyle=\mathsf{rowcnt}(S,W)
=𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍phys​(S,W,β2).\displaystyle=\mathsf{rowcnt}^{\mathrm{phys}}(S,W,\beta_{2}).

The source-sequence domain-coverage score also agrees across the class.

Proof. Apply Proposition 2 to each realization. □\square

Proposition 4 (periodic binding criterion).

Suppose TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} is a positive multiple of gg and the fixed target mapping repeats every TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} bytes up to one-to-one relabeling of domains and rows. If β=(A,E,B)∈Γ⁡(W)\beta=(A,E,B)\in\Gamma(W), then replacing BB by any base in the same residue class modulo TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} yields another tile placement in Γ⁡(W)\Gamma(W), provided that the resulting range stays inside the CU-local aperture. Placements of simultaneously resident tiles are legal when their reserved regions are also disjoint.

Formally, “up to relabeling” requires that, for each admitted base shift k​TmapkT_{\mathrm{map}}, fixed bijections on the realized domain labels and on the realized rows within each domain transform the resolved labels at address aa into those at a+k​Tmapa+kT_{\mathrm{map}} for every live address aa.

Proof. Changing the base by a multiple of TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} preserves gg-alignment and only relabels domains and rows, preserving their equality relations and hence Definition 3. The shift is bijective, so address uniqueness is preserved; the aperture and disjoint-range conditions supply the remaining placement requirements. □\square

Instantiation. The certified period of each admitted bit-field address mapping is one row-block span. Starting from the base residue used during synthesis, aligning each allocation extent to TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} preserves that residue for all contiguously packed allocations while keeping their ranges disjoint. Per-organization values of TmapT_{\mathrm{map}} are recorded in Appendix D.

A.4. Projected Row-Reuse Kernel Reduction

For the representative source-coordinate sequence SS defined above, let WDW_{D} and WRW_{R} represent the domain and row sublayouts of Definition 1. Assume rank⁡(WD)=b\operatorname{rank}(W_{D})=b. Once WDW_{D} is fixed, each domain’s first request is fixed; the remaining choice is whether later same-domain requests reuse its open row. The sequence partitions into domain-local subsequences. For every non-first request, predD⁡(i)\operatorname{pred}_{D}(i) denotes the preceding request in the same WDW_{D} domain. Under Definition 2’s closed initial state, the intrinsic source-order opening-miss count is

(12) Nmiss​(S,WD)=|{WD​ri∣0≤i<N}|=𝖼𝗈𝗏⁡(S,WD).N_{\mathrm{miss}}(S;W_{D})=\left|\{W_{D}r_{i}\mid 0\leq i<N\}\right|=\mathsf{cov}(S,W_{D}).

This count is independent of WRW_{R}. For a fixed WDW_{D}, opening misses and coverage are therefore fixed; only the hit/conflict split varies with WRW_{R}.

Because ii and predD⁡(i)\operatorname{pred}_{D}(i) have the same domain label, their difference obeys

Δi\displaystyle\Delta_{i} =ri⊕rpredD⁡(i),\displaystyle=r_{i}\oplus r_{\operatorname{pred}_{D}(i)},
WD​Δi\displaystyle W_{D}\Delta_{i} =0,\displaystyle=0,
WR​ri=WR​rpredD⁡(i)\displaystyle W_{R}r_{i}=W_{R}r_{\operatorname{pred}_{D}(i)} ⟺Δi∈ker⁡(WR)\displaystyle\Longleftrightarrow\Delta_{i}\in\ker(W_{R})
