wWD​(Δ)=|{i|predD⁡(i)​ exists and ​Δi=Δ}|.w_{W_{D}}(\Delta)=\left|\left\{i\,\middle|\,\operatorname{pred}_{D}(i)\text{ exists and }\Delta_{i}=\Delta\right\}\right|.

Summing these weights over the kernel gives the intrinsic hit count

(13) Nhit​(S,WD,K)=∑Δ∈KwWD​(Δ).N_{\mathrm{hit}}(S;W_{D},K)=\sum_{\Delta\in K}w_{W_{D}}(\Delta).

Since every request is a miss, a hit, or a conflict,

(14) Nconf​(S,WD,K)=N−Nmiss​(S,WD)−Nhit​(S,WD,K).N_{\mathrm{conf}}(S;W_{D},K)=N-N_{\mathrm{miss}}(S;W_{D})-N_{\mathrm{hit}}(S;W_{D},K).

For any completed layout W=[WC;WD;WR]W=[W_{C};W_{D};W_{R}] inducing KK, these partial-layout counts are exactly Nmiss​(S,W)N_{\mathrm{miss}}(S,W) and Nconf​(S,W)N_{\mathrm{conf}}(S,W) used by 𝗋𝗈𝗐𝖼𝗇𝗍⁡(S,W)\mathsf{rowcnt}(S,W). Equations (12)–(14) prove that, for fixed WDW_{D}, minimizing conflicts is exactly equivalent to maximizing the weighted kernel objective.

Thus the row block affects the fixed-domain score only through its row-reuse kernel KK; two row blocks inducing the same KK capture the same weighted differences. If the joint domain–row map has rank b+rrowb+r_{\mathrm{row}} and n=b+rrow+cn=b+r_{\mathrm{row}}+c, then dimK=c\dim K=c, and the fixed-domain problem is

(15) max⁡∑Δ∈KK⊆ker⁡(WD),dimK=c⁡wWD​(Δ).\max_{K\subseteq\ker(W_{D}),\ \dim K=c}\sum_{\Delta\in K}w_{W_{D}}(\Delta).

Equation (15) is the candidate-conditioned fixed-domain kernel objective used by TileDRAM. For each candidate, the target field widths and legal-placement constraints fix the admissible bb, rrowr_{\mathrm{row}}, and c=n−b−rrowc=n-b-r_{\mathrm{row}}. The next subsection gives the reduced-coordinate solver interface and its lifting correctness.

The first request to each domain is an opening miss. The two remaining requests contribute the same difference 001001, so choosing K=span⁡{001}K=\operatorname{span}\{001\} captures weight two and makes both intrinsic source-order hits.

A.5. Fixed-Domain Solver Interface

The solver operates only on the weighted same-domain predecessor differences.

After merging equal differences, choose NDN_{D} whose columns form a basis of ker⁡(WD)\ker(W_{D}). The solver represents each difference by its unique coordinate uu and searches a cc-dimensional reduced subspace K~\widetilde{K}:

ND∈𝔽2n×(n−b),im(ND)=ker(WD),K~⊆𝔽2n−b,dimK~=c,K=ND​K~:={ND​u∣u∈K~},∑u∈K~wWD​(ND​u)=∑Δ∈KwWD​(Δ).\begin{gathered}N_{D}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n\times(n-b)},\qquad\operatorname{im}(N_{D})=\ker(W_{D}),\\ \widetilde{K}\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n-b},\qquad\dim\widetilde{K}=c,\\ K=N_{D}\widetilde{K}:=\{N_{D}u\mid u\in\widetilde{K}\},\\ \sum_{u\in\widetilde{K}}w_{W_{D}}(N_{D}u)=\sum_{\Delta\in K}w_{W_{D}}(\Delta).\end{gathered}

The resulting weighted-subspace interface is the one studied by Rotaru et al. (Rotaru et al., 2025, §6.1–6.2 and §7). TileDRAM uses the cited linearized Problem 3 formulation for the exact route and its greedy construction for the greedy route. The exact route optimizes a fixed WDW_{D} on the complete positive-weight support; the greedy route is heuristic. If the returned generators span fewer than cc dimensions, they are extended to an algebraically feasible cc-dimensional subspace before lifting. Nonnegative weights ensure that this completion cannot reduce the objective. The exact route retains the highest-scoring such completion, whereas the greedy route applies its feasible completion rule.

Proposition 5 (coordinate reduction and lifting correctness).

Assume rank⁡(WD)=b\operatorname{rank}(W_{D})=b and choose NDN_{D} as above. The map K~↦ND​K~\widetilde{K}\mapsto N_{D}\widetilde{K} is a bijection from the cc-dimensional subspaces of 𝔽2n−b\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n-b} to the feasible subspaces in Eq. (15), and it preserves their objective values. Consequently, the cited exact solution lifts to a fixed-WDW_{D} optimum, while a greedy solution lifts to a feasible fixed-WDW_{D} solution.

Proof.

Because NDN_{D} has full column rank, u↦ND​uu\mapsto N_{D}u is a bijection onto ker⁡(WD)\ker(W_{D}) and preserves subspace dimension. The displayed objective identity then preserves objective order after equal differences have been merged.

□\square

A.6. Kernel-to-Layout Reconstruction

Proposition 6 (row-block reconstruction).

Let K⊆ker⁡(WD)K\subseteq\ker(W_{D}) have dimension cc, assume WDW_{D} has full row rank bb, and set rrow=n−b−cr_{\mathrm{row}}=n-b-c. Then there is a row block WR∈𝔽2rrow×nW_{R}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{r_{\mathrm{row}}\times n} such that

ker⁡([WD;WR])=K.\ker([W_{D};W_{R}])=K.

Proof. From K⊆ker⁡(WD)K\subseteq\ker(W_{D}), it follows that row⁡(WD)⊆K⟂\operatorname{row}(W_{D})\subseteq K^{\perp}. Extend a basis of row⁡(WD)\operatorname{row}(W_{D}) to a basis of K⟂K^{\perp} using rrowr_{\mathrm{row}} additional vectors, and use those vectors as the rows of WRW_{R}. Then row⁡([WD;WR])=K⟂\operatorname{row}([W_{D};W_{R}])=K^{\perp}, whose orthogonal complement is KK. □\square

To complete the semantic map, Proposition 6 provides a joint domain–row block of rank b+rrow=n−cb+r_{\mathrm{row}}=n-c. Choose cc residual-address rows that add the remaining independent directions and place them in WCW_{C}. This gives

Wsem=[WCWDWR],rank𝔽2⁡(Wsem)=n.W_{\mathrm{sem}}=\begin{bmatrix}W_{C}\\ W_{D}\\ W_{R}\end{bmatrix},\qquad\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb{F}_{2}}(W_{\mathrm{sem}})=n.

Basis extension guarantees this full-rank algebraic completion. For m>nm>n, a candidate may add m−nm-n rank-redundant residual rows; the finite catalog retains only completions satisfying the target embedding and sparsity constraints. Lemma 2 expresses each retained completion as the executable map WphysW_{\mathrm{phys}}.

A.7. Certified-Catalog Selection

Domain-block enumeration followed by kernel and residual-address reconstruction generates layout candidates. Target realization, mapping-consistency, and binding-legality checks retain the single finite certified catalog 𝒲cert\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}} defined above.

The complete lexicographic selection functional is

(16) J⁡(S,W)=(Nconf​(S,W),−𝖼𝗈𝗏⁡(S,WD),nnz⁡(G−1​W)).J(S,W)=\bigl(N_{\mathrm{conf}}(S,W),-\mathsf{cov}(S,W_{D}),\operatorname{nnz}(G^{-1}W)\bigr).

The first coordinate minimizes source-order row conflicts. The second favors greater source-sequence domain coverage from Eq. (9), and the last is a nonzero-term complexity proxy for the executable linear address map.

Proposition 7 (catalog-relative exactness).

Under Definition 4’s assumption N>0N>0, let

𝒲cert\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}} be nonempty. By its definition, every member is certified, preserves request formation, and has a nonempty legal tile-placement set. Exhaustive comparison returning

W⋆∈arg​minW∈𝒲cert⁡J​(S,W)W^{\star}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{W\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}}}J(S,W)

is exact for the lexicographic objective over the emitted catalog. With the exact inner route on the complete positive-weight support, the kernel emitted for each retained WDW_{D} is also optimal for its fixed-domain algebraic problem. With the greedy inner route, each emitted kernel is feasible and exhaustive comparison remains exact over the resulting catalog.

Proof. Definition 2 supplies the common ordered sequence, and Proposition 2 makes each certified realization agree on the conflict coordinate; Definition 4 and mapping consistency preserve the source-sequence domain-coverage score. The final coordinate is computed directly from the emitted physical map. Proposition 5 supplies the exact or feasible fixed-domain result for the chosen inner route. Since the catalog is finite and nonempty, exhaustive comparison attains the catalog’s lexicographic minimum. □\square

A.8. Applicability Conditions

The construction and its source-order analysis apply to recurring tiled access patterns whose admitted instances satisfy three conditions; tiled GEMM is the evaluated instance in this paper.

(C1) Recurring ordered sequence.

For every W∈𝒲certW\in\mathcal{W}_{\mathrm{cert}}, the source interpretation yields the same coordinate sequence for all β∈Γ⁡(W)\beta\in\Gamma(W), and request formation preserves the one-request-per-event correspondence, event order, and coordinate ancestry. This makes the row-state trajectory well defined and amortizes the cost of one offline selection across the recurring tile placements.

(C2) Linear live-coordinate representation. The source interpretation maps live layout units injectively into 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, and the compiler expresses the resulting coordinate projection as a Linear Layout. With a selected full-column-rank tile-to-DRAM Linear Layout, distinct live units therefore remain distinguishable under composition.

(C3) Certified target realization. On the admitted live image, the within-unit byte offset affects only byte/column position, while byte placement and the fixed DRAM address mapping produce affine domain and row labels with the rank conditions of Lemma 2 and the consistency of Definition 3. The modeled intrinsic source-order state transition retains one open row per domain until a request to that domain replaces it.

Together, these conditions justify the ordered row-buffer semantics and fixed-domain kernel reduction. Given a nonempty finite certified catalog, the selector is well-defined. For an emitted cc-dimensional kernel, its captured same-domain predecessor-difference weight is exactly the source-order row reuse from Eq. (13).

Appendix B Controller-Side DRAM Address Mapping: Configuration Feasibility, Construction Scale, and Performance

Controller-side address mapping supplies one global interpretation for every request served by the target memory controller. We evaluate fixed global hashes that apply the same static bit-mixing rule to every operand stream, regardless of its operand properties or tile access signature. TileDRAM retains the target controller mapping and selects a tile-to-DRAM layout for each tile access signature.

The experiments below separate construction cost from mapping effectiveness. Section B.2 evaluates the Rotaru-style exhaustive full-trace search, whose outer mapping choice makes trace construction candidate-dependent.

B.1. Fixed Global Mappings: Closure and Replay Feasibility

The fixed-hash family covers row-to-bank, column-to-bank, bank-to-row, and column-to-row XOR mappings, compound row/bank swizzling, and a field swizzle styled after Ramulator2’s MOP4CLXOR address mapper (Luo et al., 2024). Every recipe applies one frozen rule to both operand access sequences. Compilation checks whether the rule closes over the live address domain; replay-complete entries then execute through the same Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 path as conventional placement and TileDRAM. The fixed-hash replay uses a Llama 4 up/gate projection with tile (B​M,B​N,B​K)=(64,128,64)(BM,BN,BK)=(64,128,64) under the t8/b16/row13/col3 organization with open-row FR-FCFS. The conventional branch uses the identity RoBaTiCoCh mapping (Row–Bank–Tier–Column–Channel), realized by Ramulator2’s RoBaRaCoCh mapper.

The best evaluated replay-complete fixed global recipes reduce conflicts by only 0.0892% and improve performance by 0.0144%. The fixed mappings encode one address-field transformation for the complete access sequence, whereas TileDRAM selects placement from the ordered accesses of each signature.

B.2. Cost of Rotaru-Style Exhaustive Full-Trace Synthesis

The multi-bank mapping synthesis of Rotaru et al. (Rotaru et al., 2025) uses a complete workload trace as its specialization unit and treats the domain mapping as an outer search variable. After fixing an outer mapping, the trace is compressed into weighted same-domain predecessor differences for the fixed-domain Problem 3 solver. Changing the outer mapping changes request-domain membership, same-domain predecessors, and therefore the resulting difference histogram. Trace construction is thus candidate-dependent: a separate fixed-domain Problem 3 instance must be reconstructed for every outer candidate before its inner subspace solve.

For the evaluated organization, the source coordinate spans n=23n=23 bits and the target requires b=7b=7 tier-and-bank dimensions, corresponding to 128 row-buffer domains for a full-rank WDW_{D}. The bit-selecting family then contains 245,157 candidates for WDW_{D}, while the structured-XOR family contributes 105,417,617 raw candidates. Together they yield 105,662,774 outer candidates before rank filtering and row-space deduplication. Applying this search directly to the Llama 4 full trace with 7,864,320 active-lane copy events would perform approximately 8.31×10148.31\times 10^{14} evaluations of candidate copy events before any fixed-domain Problem 3 solve, full-map completion, or physical address-mapping evaluation.

At a sustained aggregate rate of 10 billion evaluations of candidate copy events per second on a large multicore CPU, this construction requires approximately 23.1 hours; at 1 billion evaluations per second, it requires approximately 9.6 days. These throughput-based estimates quantify raw outer construction before Problem 3 solves, map completion, or physical address-mapping evaluation. The outer construction alone therefore makes Rotaru-style exhaustive full-trace controller-map synthesis computationally prohibitive as a routine per-configuration path at the MoE FFN scale. Each new phase, problem shape, or autotuned tile configuration supplies a new workload-wide specialization target.

These experiments separate synthesis tractability from mapping effectiveness. Fixed global hashes are inexpensive but produce negligible changes in the evaluated replay. Rotaru-style exhaustive full-trace synthesis explores a much larger mapping space, but its candidate-dependent outer construction is computationally prohibitive at this scale. TileDRAM instead changes the specialization granularity: it keeps the controller mapping fixed and reuses placement selected per recurring tile access signature.

Appendix C Compiler Interface

Listing 1 shows an excerpt from the programmer-facing tiled GEMM kernel used by the compiler path in Section 5.1. The annotation exposes tiled-kernel semantics used by the compiler, while the kernel body uses ordinary tiled loads and matrix multiplication; the output-store path is omitted for brevity.

Tile-access and binding metadata.

For each tile access signature, the compiler records the operand-property tuple, comprising operand position (lhs or rhs), data type (dtype), source-stride pattern (stride), and source layout (row-major or column-major), together with the access shape and address space needed by the lowered path, and routes the resulting source pointer tensor through APPLY. Compiler-side BIND performs template lookup and records the selected target-specific layout template together with the rule for deriving the tile ID from the current execution context. When that tile is placed in a DRAM region, runtime BIND obtains the referenced template from this binding metadata and combines it with the concrete tile ID, source interval, and concrete DRAM region to construct its tile descriptor for that region. Runtime BIND passes the descriptor for the active resident tile as a runtime input to APPLY.

Address-lowering sequence.

For each admitted operand access, lowering places the APPLY path after the source pointer tensor is formed by address arithmetic. At execution, the path extracts the source-relative coordinates, separates the layout-unit index from the within-unit byte offset, applies the 𝔽2\mathbb{F}_{2}-linear map, affine XOR translation, and byte placement, then reconstructs the backend address while retaining that offset. Shifts, masks, XOR, parity, and address arithmetic implement this sequence before the original asynchronous copy.

The compiler records the canonical address-function associated with each transformed tile access signature. The compiler-side template reference and runtime BIND connect the programmer-facing kernel intent, the lowered compiler realization, and the simulator descriptor recorded by the cross-path equivalence artifact.

Appendix D Artifact and Evaluation Configuration

The artifact supports the three result groups reported in this paper: the 108-case MoE full suite and hardware cost calibration, the controller-mapping comparisons in Appendix B, and the six-organization retargeting sweep. It records the revisions, build options, simulator configuration files, trace manifests, and run manifests that determine the reported results.

Software surface.

The artifact pins the TileDRAM source tree, Accel-Sim/GPGPU-Sim build, Ramulator2 checkout, Triton/Gluon compiler tree, CUDA and NVBit environment, Python package set, host OS, C++ compiler, and simulator build flags. The run manifests bind these fields to trace collection, layout selection, descriptor construction, and replay for each result group. All reported TileDRAM layouts are selected by the greedy route on the complete positive-weight support (Appendix A.5). Per-case synthesis-resource records support the offline layout-synthesis cost reported below; controller-mapping manifests support the comparisons in Appendix B.

Cross-path equivalence artifact.

The artifact includes a hash-closed compiler–simulator execution-equivalence report. For every semantic address-function family, the report records the representative descriptor and descriptor-table hashes, canonical function hash, per-operand compiler transformation-binding and lowered-IR hashes, compiler binary hash, production transformer binary hash, structural-vector hash, and mismatch count. The release gate passes only when the canonical evaluator, lowered compiler IR, and production simulator transformer produce identical addresses for every reported vector. The current report admits all 108 main-suite configurations and covers the identity and selected-layout branches: 216 runtime descriptor tables (one per configuration per branch, each covering both input operands), 2,118,464 descriptors counted at per-tile-instance granularity, 378 semantic address-function families, and 45,460 structural byte addresses with zero mismatches.

Compiler-cost calibration artifact.

The hardware calibration uses the same 108 full-GEMM kernel configurations as the main suite, spanning six model families and eight tile shapes. The selected templates supply the address computation for both operands. Each case records H​0H0 without address transformation, H​1H1 with identity address generation, and H​2H2 with the selected transformation; only H​2/H​1−1H2/H1-1 enters the reported overhead. Each mode contributes 51 measurements under a rotating six-order schedule and an adaptively sized timing window of at least 10 ms. The artifact records the case, template, generated-code, binary, and calibration-harness hashes together with the lowering report, resource report, SASS dump, and timing samples. The publication gate validates all 108 cases. The resulting transformation-versus-identity overhead is 0.17% geomean, below 0.01% median, 0.57% at the 95th percentile, and 4.93% maximum.

Offline layout-synthesis cost.

TileDRAM performs one offline synthesis per case, producing the layouts for its tile access signatures and amortizing the synthesis cost across their dynamic tile instances. Across the 108-case solver-cost campaign, the measured median per-case synthesis time is 349.0 s and the measured median peak resident memory is 227.0 MB. The artifact records the solver route, wall time, peak resident memory, and completion status for each case.

Platform.

GPU-side traces are collected from Triton and Gluon tiled GEMM kernels using NVBit (Tillet et al., 2019; , 2026; Villa et al., 2019) and replayed in a trace-driven Accel-Sim/Ramulator2 platform. Accel-Sim supplies the GPU execution context, including warp issue, instruction replay, memory stalls, and cycle accounting. Ramulator2 supplies the 3D DRAM backend, including address mapping, command scheduling, row-buffer state, read latency, and foreground queue wait. Appendix B separately specifies the controller-mapping alternatives used in the controller-mapping comparison.

Replay contract.

Each baseline–TileDRAM pair is constructed from one CU-local access sequence and one target DRAM organization. The paired fields are the kernel shape, tile shape, execution staging, source trace, target organization, and fixed DRAM address mapping; each branch records its observed source ingress and controller service orders. The treatment field is DRAM placement: baseline uses conventional placement, while TileDRAM uses the selected tile-to-DRAM layout for the same target organization.

Main workload set.

The primary MoE full suite contains 108 full-trace FFN cases from Qwen3 (Qwen Team, 2025), DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI, 2024), Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (Qwen Team, 2026), Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026), Hunyuan-A13B (Tencent Hunyuan Team, 2025), and Llama 4 (Meta AI, 2025), with 18 cases per family. Each family contributes one up/gate and one down projection, and each projection is measured at M=64M=64 over the four tiles 64×64×3264{\times}64{\times}32, 64×128×3264{\times}128{\times}32, 64×128×6464{\times}128{\times}64, 64×256×3264{\times}256{\times}32 and at M=128M=128 over the five tiles 64×64×3264{\times}64{\times}32, 128×128×32128{\times}128{\times}32, 128×128×64128{\times}128{\times}64, 128×256×64128{\times}256{\times}64, 128×256×128128{\times}256{\times}128, giving eight M=64M=64 and ten M=128M=128 cases per family over eight distinct tile shapes; 64×64×3264{\times}64{\times}32 is the one shape shared by both MM groups, so it carries 24 of the 108 cases while each other shape carries 12. The suite also supplies the complete hardware address-transformation cost cohort. The artifact records the problem size, tile size, operand properties, including operand position, data type, source-stride pattern, and source layout, and model-family identifiers for each case. The retargeting sweep uses six full-trace FFN streams with shapes (64,4096,1536)(64,4096,1536), (64,4096,7168)(64,4096,7168), (64,4096,3072)(64,4096,3072), (128,8192,5120)(128,8192,5120), (128,3584,3072)(128,3584,3072), and (128,512,2048)(128,512,2048), all with 64×64×3264{\times}64{\times}32 tiles and one pipeline stage.

Memory-system configurations.

All modeled organizations use OpenRowPolicy and FR-FCFS. The full suite, fixed-hash supplement, and retargeting sweep use RoBaTiCoCh (Row–Bank–Tier–Column–Channel), realized by Ramulator2’s RoBaRaCoCh mapper. The full suite uses 8 tiers, 16 banks, 13 row bits, and 3 column bits. Refresh is enabled for every replay in the 108-case full suite. The fixed-hash supplement uses the same tier/bank counts with 13 row bits and 3 column bits, as stated in Appendix B. For the main organization, the address-mapping byte period is one row-block span, Tmap=128×512T_{\mathrm{map}}=128\times 512 bytes={}={}64 KiB; the corresponding spans for the retargeting organizations follow from their own domain counts and row sizes. In particular, the two row12/col4 organizations use 1-KiB rows and periods of 32 KiB and 128 KiB; the run manifests record the value used for each organization. The evaluated operand access sequence is an ordered tile-local access sequence of active-lane copy events generated by LDGSTS.128; operand-tile source-coordinate sequences are the optimization inputs, and all copy event and row-event counts use this same event granularity. Because the CU-local aperture path has neither cross-CU request merging nor a coalescing stage (Section 2.1), each active-lane LDGSTS.128 event is one 16-byte request at the stack boundary, and both replay arms share this granularity.

Controller-mapping artifacts.

The artifact records each fixed-hash operation, scope, closure result, compile score, replay manifest, and the separate operand-scoped diagnostic entry for Appendix B.

Metric definitions.

The request-weighted row-conflict rate is the pooled conflict count divided by all pooled row events. Pooled row-conflict reduction uses the corresponding summed baseline and TileDRAM conflict counts. For performance, each matched case contributes one speedup,

𝑆𝑈i=Cbaseline,iCTileDRAM,i,𝑆𝑈geo=(∏i∈𝒮𝑆𝑈i)1/|𝒮|.\mathit{SU}_{i}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{baseline},i}}{C_{\mathrm{TileDRAM},i}},\qquad\mathit{SU}_{\mathrm{geo}}=\left(\prod_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\mathit{SU}_{i}\right)^{1/|\mathcal{S}|}.

Speedup is reported as the geometric mean of per-case baseline-to-TileDRAM cycle ratios. Replay reports simulator-backed memory-system performance; RQ4 separately reports the hardware-measured address-transformation cost (Section 6.5). For organization oo, we also report the pooled-cycle speedup

Po=∑i∈𝒲oCbaseline,i,o∑i∈𝒲oCTileDRAM,i,o,\mathit{P}_{o}=\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{W}_{o}}C_{\mathrm{baseline},i,o}}{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{W}_{o}}C_{\mathrm{TileDRAM},i,o}},

where 𝒲o\mathcal{W}_{o} contains the six workload streams evaluated under oo. This organization-level pooled ratio is distinct from the six-stream geometric mean; the pooled-cycle range in RQ3 is the minimum and maximum of Po\mathit{P}_{o} across the six organizations.

Reported metrics.

The replay records row hits, row misses, row conflicts, row-buffer hit rate, row-conflict rate, Ramulator2 average read latency, foreground queue wait, shader memory-stall cycles, and cycles. The formal opening-miss count is a source-order, closed-domain quantity; replay row-miss counters are service-order observables that can also reflect refresh and controller behavior. The 108-case MoE full suite reports 75.7% baseline and 15.2% TileDRAM row-conflict rates, an 80.0% pooled reduction, and a 1.77×\times geomean speedup. Across the same cases, shader-memory stalls fall by 53.9% and request-weighted Ramulator2 read latency falls by 49.6%. The retargeting experiment reports 36 paired cases across six 3D DRAM organizations, with pooled row-conflict reduction of 79.2% and geomean speedup of 2.20×\times.
